segments.text: THE STATE OF TEXAS v. AMBER GUYGER
Botham Jean  ·  26  ·  killed in his own home
segments.vo: She was a Dallas police officer. Sworn to protect. And on the night of September sixth, twenty-eighteen, she walked through a door that wasn't hers, and killed the man who lived behind it. His name was Botham Jean. Twenty-six years old. Sitting in his own living room, eating a bowl of ice cream. He wasn't a suspect. He wasn't armed. He had done nothing wrong. He was simply home. The officer said it was a mistake. That she thought his apartment was hers. For thirteen months, that one sentence was her entire defense. But inside that courtroom, the mistake she kept explaining became the very thing that convicted her.

Before this becomes a story about a police officer, it has to be a story about the man she killed, because the system almost let everyone forget him. Botham Shem Jean grew up on the island of Saint Lucia. He came to the United States for college, graduated from Harding University, and worked as an accountant at one of the biggest firms in the world. He sang in his church. By twenty-eighteen he was living in Dallas, on the fourth floor of an apartment complex called the South Side Flats. Apartment fourteen seventy-eight. A secure building. The kind of place you rent so you can feel safe when you close your door at night.

On the evening of September sixth, there was nothing unusual. Just a young man home alone, eating ice cream on his couch. Remember that image, because everything that is about to happen happened to a man who had done absolutely nothing.
segments.image_query: South Side Flats Dallas apartment building

segments.vo: Amber Guyger had been a Dallas police officer for around four years. That night she was coming off a long shift, still in her uniform, still armed. She parked on the wrong floor. The fourth. One level above her own. Every floor mirrored the one beneath it. Same doors. Same numbers, one digit apart. She walked to his door believing it was hers. Minutes later, she called nine one one.
Listen closely. Again and again, she repeats the same three words. And notice what is missing, the name of the man bleeding on his own floor.
segments.text: "I thought it was my apartment" — repeated ~20x

segments.vo: When the responding officers arrived, their body cameras were recording. This is not the officer who fired, she was off duty, and there is no camera on the shooting itself. This is the aftermath.
segments.query: Amber Guyger bodycam Botham Jean shooting

segments.vo: The building's own cameras told part of the story she couldn't. Watch her path that night. The wrong floor. The wrong hallway. The wrong door.

And then there is the detail the prosecution would never let the jury forget. Outside Botham Jean's door was a bright red doormat. His door had one. Hers did not. One glance down, one, and the story of a simple, innocent mistake begins to fall apart.
Under questioning, the prosecutors took her own version, the one she had told over and over, and walked it backward, one step at a time.

segments.text: You can't defend a home that was never yours
segments.vo: The defense leaned on the Castle Doctrine, the right to defend your own home. But there was one problem the law would not move around. It wasn't her home. You cannot claim the right to defend a home you entered by mistake. The very doctrine she was leaning on required the one thing she did not have.

segments.vo: Four things before we go. One. Amber Guyger remains in a Texas prison. Two. Botham Jean's family pursued accountability beyond the criminal trial. Three. His mother turned her grief into a fight for police accountability that did not end when the trial did. And four. Every time an officer now says the word mistake in a courtroom, somewhere a prosecutor remembers a red doormat, a bowl of ice cream, and a young man who was killed for the crime of being home. Rest in peace, Botham Jean. If this story mattered to you, subscribe, because holding power to the same law as everyone else is the entire reason this channel exists.
